claim: The human AdipoR1 and AdipoR2 proteins, as well as their C. elegans homolog PAQR-2, protect against cell membrane rigidification by exogenous saturated fatty acids by regulating phospholipid composition.
source: The human AdipoR1 and AdipoR2 proteins, as well as their C. elegans homolog PAQR-2, protect against cell membrane rigidification by exogenous saturated fatty acids by regulating phospholipid composition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of established knowledge from prior work.

claim: Mutations in the C. elegans gene acs-13 suppress the phenotypes of paqr-2 mutant worms, including their characteristic membrane fluidity defects.
source: Here, we show that mutations in the C. elegans gene acs-13 help to suppress the phenotypes of paqr-2 mutant worms, including their characteristic membrane fluidity defects.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: acs-13 encodes a homolog of the human acyl-CoA synthetase ACSL1.
source: acs-13 encodes a homolog of the human acyl-CoA synthetase ACSL1
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by sequence homology analysis.

claim: ACS-13 localizes to the mitochondrial membrane where it likely activates long chain fatty acids for import and degradation.
source: acs-13 encodes a homolog of the human acyl-CoA synthetase ACSL1, and localizes to the mitochondrial membrane where it likely activates long chains fatty acids for import and degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by localization experiments and Western blotting data in the manuscript.

claim: Silencing ACSL1 in human cells protects against the membrane rigidifying effects of palmitate.
source: Using siRNA combined with lipidomics and membrane fluidity assays (FRAP and Laurdan dye staining) we further show that the human ACSL1 potentiates lipotoxicity by the saturated fatty acid palmitate: silencing ACSL1 protects against the membrane rigidifying effects of palmitate
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by FRAP and Laurdan dye experiments in HEK293 cells.

claim: ACSL1 silencing acts as a suppressor of AdipoR2 knockdown in human cells.
source: silencing ACSL1 protects against the membrane rigidifying effects of palmitate and acts as a suppressor of AdipoR2 knockdown
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by FRAP experiments showing that ACSL1 siRNA prevents membrane rigidification in AdipoR2 knockdown cells.

claim: acs-13 mutations in C. elegans and ACSL1 knockdown in human cells prevent lipotoxicity by promoting increased levels of polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing phospholipids.
source: We conclude that acs-13 mutations in C. elegans and ACSL1 knockdown in human cells prevent lipotoxicity by promoting increased levels of polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing phospholipids.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by lipidomics data showing increased PUFA levels in phospholipids.

claim: Lipotoxicity occurs when fatty acids, especially saturated fatty acids such as palmitate, accumulate at excessive levels in cells or plasma.
source: Lipotoxicity occurs when fatty acids, especially saturated fatty acids such as palmitate, accumulate at excessive levels in cells or plasma (Mota et al., 2016; Palomer et al., 2018; Schaffer, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Liver steatosis, beta cell failure and endothelial cell defects are caused by lipotoxicity and are important health complications associated with obesity and diabetes.
source: In particular, liver steatosis, beta cell failure and endothelial cell defects are caused by lipotoxicity and are important health complications associated with obesity and diabetes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: A primary mechanism of lipotoxicity relates to membrane rigidification caused by an excess of saturated fatty acids incorporation into membrane phospholipids.
source: Additionally, recent evidence suggests that a primary mechanism of lipotoxicity relates to membrane rigidification caused by an excess of saturated fatty acids (SFAs) incorporation into membrane phospholipids.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Adipocytes must promote fatty acid desaturation in order to prevent membrane rigidification and lipotoxity by palmitate.
source: For example, adipocytes must promote fatty acid desaturation in order to prevent membrane rigidification and lipotoxity by palmitate (Collins et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Two recent genome-wide gene silencing/knockout screens identified regulators of SFA incorporation into phospholipids as key determinants of palmitate toxicity in human cells.
source: Also, two recent genome-wide gene silencing/knockout screens identified regulators of SFA incorporation into phospholipids as key determinants of palmitate toxicity in human cells (Piccolis et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The gene paqr-2 in C. elegans encodes a homolog of the mammalian AdipoR1 and AdipoR2.
source: In C. elegans, the gene paqr-2 encodes a homolog of the mammalian AdipoR1 and AdipoR2 (seven transmembrane domain proteins localized to the plasma membrane with their N-terminus within the cytosol and likely acting as hydrolases; Holland et al., 2011; Pei et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 1996; Tang et al., 2005; Yamauchi et al., 2003)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: PAQR-2 acts together with its dedicated partner IGLR-2 to sense and respond to membrane rigidification by promoting fatty acid desaturation until membrane fluidity is restored to optimal levels.
source: and acts together with its dedicated partner IGLR-2 (a single-pass plasma membrane protein with a large extracellular domain containing one immunoglobulin domain and several leucine-rich repeats) to sense and respond to membrane rigidification by promoting fatty acid desaturation until membrane fluidity is restored to optimal levels (Svensson et al., 2011; Svensk et al., 2013; Svensk et al., 2016a; Devkota et al., 2017; Bodhicharla et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Wild-type worms are unaffected by the presence of SFAs in their diet, but paqr-2(tm3410) or iglr-2(et34) null mutants are extremely SFA-sensitive.
source: Wild-type worms are unaffected by the presence of SFAs in their diet, but paqr-2(tm3410) or iglr-2(et34) null mutants are extremely SFA-sensitive: inclusion of SFAs in the diet of the mutant rapidly leads to excess SFAs in membrane phospholipids, membrane rigidification and death.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge from prior work.

claim: PAQR-2 and IGLR-2 are essential for the ability of C. elegans to grow at low temperatures such as 15°C because they are required to sense cold-induced rigidification and promote fatty acid desaturation until membrane fluidity is restored.
source: Both proteins are integral plasma membrane proteins that are also essential for the ability of C. elegans to grow at low temperatures such as 15°C because they are required to sense cold-induced rigidification and promote fatty acid desaturation until membrane fluidity is restored (Svensk et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The paqr-2(tm3410) and iglr-2(et34) mutant phenotypes include a withered appearance of the thin membranous tail tip.
source: The paqr-2(tm3410) and iglr-2(et34) mutant phenotypes also include a withered appearance of the thin membranous tail tip (Svensson et al., 2011; Svensk et al., 2016b)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: All paqr-2 and iglr-2 mutant phenotypes can be attenuated or fully suppressed by secondary mutations in other genes that cause increased fatty acid desaturation.
source: and all mutant phenotypes can be attenuated or fully suppressed by secondary mutations in other genes that cause increased fatty acid desaturation (Svensk et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: paqr-2 and iglr-2 mutant phenotypes can be suppressed by mutations that cause increased incorporation of potently fluidizing long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LCPUFAs) into phospholipids.
source: or increased incorporation of potently fluidizing long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LCPUFAs; fatty acids with 18 carbons or more and two or more double bonds) into phospholipids (Ruiz et al., 2018)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The paqr-2(tm3410) and iglr-2(et34) mutant phenotypes can be partially suppressed by the inclusion of fluidizing concentrations of nonionic detergents in the culture plate.
source: Additionally, the paqr-2(tm3410) and iglr-2(et34) mutant phenotypes can be partially suppressed by the inclusion of fluidizing concentrations of nonionic detergents in the culture plate (Svensk et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The acs-13(et54) allele carries a glycine-to-arginine amino acid substitution at position 125 (G125R).
source: The acs-13(et54) allele carries a glycine-to-arginine amino acid substitution at position 125 (G125R), within the proposed N-terminal cytoplasmic domain of the ACS-13 protein
evidence: This is stated in the results section and confirmed by sequencing data.

claim: The G125R mutation in acs-13(et54) is within the proposed N-terminal cytoplasmic domain of the ACS-13 protein.
source: The acs-13(et54) allele carries a glycine-to-arginine amino acid substitution at position 125 (G125R), within the proposed N-terminal cytoplasmic domain of the ACS-13 protein, which also contains two predicted transmembrane domains presumed by homology to be embedded in organelles such a mitochondria or ER
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on protein modeling.

claim: acs-13(et54) is a loss-of-function mutation.
source: That acs-13(et54) is a loss-of-function mutation was confirmed in several ways.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by multiple experimental approaches including CRISPR/Cas9 validation.

claim: The same G125R mutation and other loss-of-function alleles of acs-13 created using CRISPR/Cas9 greatly improve the ability of paqr-2(tm3410) mdt-15(et14) double mutants to grow on 20 mM glucose.
source: Firstly, the same G125R mutation and other loss-of-function alleles of acs-13 were created using CRISPR/Cas9 and found to greatly improve the ability of paqr-2(tm3410) mdt-15(et14) double mutants to grow on 20 mM glucose (Figure 1C–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: acs-13(et54) and acs-13(ok2861) both greatly enhance the ability of mdt-15(et14) to suppress the glucose and cold intolerance of the paqr-2 mutant.
source: Secondly, the acs-13(et54) and acs-13(ok2861), a deletion allele of acs-13 obtained from the C. elegans Genetics Center, both greatly enhance the ability of mdt-15(et14) to suppress the glucose and cold intolerance of the paqr-2 mutant (Figure 1E–F; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1E-F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: acs-13(et54) acts as an enhancer of cept-1(et10), which is another partial paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor that acts by promoting fatty acid desaturation.
source: acs-13(et54) also acts as an enhancer of cept-1(et10), which is another partial paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor that acts by promoting fatty acid desaturation
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by experimental data.

claim: acs-13(et54) does not act as an enhancer of nhr-49(et8) which is already a very potent paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor.
source: but not as an enhancer of nhr-49(et8) which is already a very potent paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor (Svensk et al., 2013; Svensk et al., 2016a)
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: acs-13(et54) does not enhance hacd-1(et12) which is a relatively poor paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor.
source: nor of hacd-1(et12) which is a relatively poor paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor (Svensk et al., 2013; Svensk et al., 2016a) and does not by itself suppress the glucose intolerance (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations and data in Figure 1G.

claim: The ability of acs-13(et54) to enhance the effects of both mdt-15(et14) and cept-1(et10) suggests that it requires the elevated UFA levels characteristic of these mutants in order to carry out its paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor function.
source: The ability of acs-13(et54) to enhance the effects of both mdt-15(et14) and cept-1(et10) suggests that it requires the elevated UFA levels characteristic of these mutants (Svensk et al., 2013) in order to carry out its paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor function.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the results section based on the experimental data and prior knowledge.

claim: acs-13(et54) or acs-13(ok2861) are not by themselves effective suppressors of the paqr-2 mutant glucose and cold intolerance nor of its characteristic withered tail tip defect.
source: Indeed, acs-13(et54) or acs-13(ok2861) are not by themselves effective suppressors of the paqr-2 mutant glucose and cold intolerance nor of its characteristic withered tail tip defect (Figure 1E–F; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C and E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in multiple figures.

claim: acs-13(et54) can by itself partially suppress the brood size defect of the paqr-2(tm3410) mutant, though not as effectively as mdt-15(et14).
source: On the other hand, acs-13(et54) can by itself partially suppress the brood size defect of the paqr-2(tm3410) mutant, though not as effectively as mdt-15(et14), and does not suppress the defecation rate or life span defects (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-C.

claim: acs-13(et54) is by itself a weak paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor but an enhancer of the UFA-producing mdt-15(et14) allele as a paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor.
source: Thus acs-13(et54) is by itself a weak paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor but an enhancer of the UFA-producing mdt-15(et14) allele as a paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the results section based on the experimental data.

claim: acs-13(et54) enhances the protective effect of the PUFA linoleic acid (18:2) when paqr-2(tm3410) mutant worms are challenged with 2 mM palmitate.
source: Additionally, acs-13(et54) enhances the protective effect of the PUFA linoleic acid (18:2) when paqr-2(tm3410) mutant worms are challenged with 2 mM palmitate (a 16:0 SFA), which further indicates a synergistic interaction between PUFA availability and acs-13(et54) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: Restoring expression of wild-type ACS-13 isoform 'a' using a cDNA transgene driven from the acs-13 promoter restores glucose intolerance in paqr-2(tm3410) mdt-15(et14); acs-13(et54) triple mutants.
source: Restoring expression of wild-type ACS-13 isoform 'a' using a cDNA transgene driven from the acs-13 promoter restores glucose intolerance (glucose is here again used as an expedient way to provide an SFA-rich diet since it is converted to SFAs by the dietary E. coli; Devkota et al., 2017) in paqr-2(tm3410) mdt-15(et14); acs-13(et54) triple mutants, which confirms the functionality of the isoform 'a' used in this study (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2A-C.

claim: ACS-13::GFP exhibits GFP-localization specifically on the mitochondria of intestinal and hypodermal cells and co-localizes with Mitotracker Deep Red.
source: The same construct modified to carry GFP fused at the C-terminal end of the ACS-13 protein exhibits GFP-localization specifically on the mitochondria of intestinal and hypodermal cells and co-localizes with Mitotracker Deep Red (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 2D.

claim: ACS-13::GFP does not co-localize with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) marker mCherry::SP12.
source: but not with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) marker mCherry::SP12 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Detection of ACS-13 protein using Western blotting of cytosol, microsome and mitochondria-enriched subcellular fractions is consistent with the mitochondrial localization of the ACS-13::GFP protein.
source: Detection of ACS-13 protein using Western blotting of cytosol, microsome and mitochondria-enriched subcellular fractions is also consistent with the mitochondrial localization of the ACS-13::GFP protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Expression of acs-13 is unaltered in paqr-2 mutants but decreased in worms carrying the gain-of-function mdt-15(et14) allele.
source: Expression of acs-13 was determined by qPCR and found to be unaltered in paqr-2 mutants but decreased in worms carrying the gain-of-function mdt-15(et14) allele (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that it may be a negatively regulated downstream target of activated MDT-15.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The morphology of the mitochondria was often visibly abnormal in acs-13(et54) mutants.
source: Additionally, the morphology of the mitochondria was often visibly abnormal in acs-13(et54) mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: An acs-13 promoter-driven transcriptional reporter shows strong expression in the intestine and hypodermis.
source: and an acs-13 promoter-driven transcriptional reporter shows strong expression in the intestine and hypodermis (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 2E.

claim: ACS-13 is localized to mitochondria in intestine and hypodermis.
source: We conclude that ACS-13 is localized to mitochondria in intestine and hypodermis, that its expression is influenced by MDT-15 and that it contributes to maintenance of mitochondria morphology.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: ACS-13 expression is influenced by MDT-15.
source: We conclude that ACS-13 is localized to mitochondria in intestine and hypodermis, that its expression is influenced by MDT-15 and that it contributes to maintenance of mitochondria morphology.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on qPCR data.

claim: ACS-13 contributes to maintenance of mitochondria morphology.
source: We conclude that ACS-13 is localized to mitochondria in intestine and hypodermis, that its expression is influenced by MDT-15 and that it contributes to maintenance of mitochondria morphology.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on observations of abnormal mitochondria morphology in acs-13 mutants.

claim: The most potent mdt-15(et14) enhancers among acyl-CoA synthetases tested by RNAi were the ACSL1/5/6 homologs acs-5 and acs-15, followed by the ACSF2 homolog acs-16.
source: The most potent mdt-15(et14) enhancers were the ACSL1/5/6 homologs acs-5 and acs-15, followed by the ACSF2 homolog acs-16 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by RNAi screening data in Figure 3A.

claim: The loss-of-function acs-5(ok2668) allele is an enhancer of mdt-15(et14).
source: We obtained the loss-of-function acs-5(ok2668) allele from the C. elegans Genetics Center and found that it is indeed an enhancer of mdt-15(et14) (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3B-C.

claim: acs-5(ok2668) did not by itself act as a paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor.
source: Like acs-13(et54), acs-5(ok2668) did not by itself act as a paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,D and G)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,D and G.

claim: acs-5(ok2668) is not as potent an mdt-15(et14) enhancer as acs-13(et54) in suppressing the glucose intolerance.
source: and is not as potent an mdt-15(et14) enhancer as acs-13(et54) in suppressing the glucose intolerance (Figure 3B–C), which likely explains why only the latter was isolated in our forward genetics screen for mdt-15(et14) enhancers.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3B-C.

claim: acs-13(et54) does not cause upregulation of the Δ9 desaturase FAT-7.
source: This is indeed the case: expression of a GFP translational reporter for the Δ9 desaturase FAT-7 is markedly increased in the presence of the mdt-15(et14) allele but unaffected by the acs-13(et54) allele either by itself or in the paqr-2(tm3410) or paqr-2(et54) mdt-15(et14) mutant backgrounds (Figure 4A–B; a larger version of Figure 4A is presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by GFP reporter data in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The ability of acs-13(et54) to act as an enhancer of mdt-15(et14) is dependent on the activity of desaturases.
source: However, the ability of acs-13(et54) to act as an enhancer of mdt-15(et14) is dependent on the activity of desaturases since their inhibition by RNAi significantly impairs the 15°C growth of paqr-2 mdt-15(et14); acs-13(et54) triple mutants, with fat-6 and fat-7 being particularly important (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by RNAi data in Figure 4C.

claim: Presence of the acs-13(et54) allele by itself or in the paqr-2 mdt-15(et14) background caused a marked increase in LCPUFAs (e.g. 20:3, 20:4 and 20:5) at the expense of shorter SFAs or MUFAs (e.g. 15:0, 16:0 and 16:1) on NGM plates.
source: Examining more specifically each type of fatty acid in PEs, we found that presence of the acs-13(et54) allele by itself or in the paqr-2 mdt-15(et14) background caused a marked increase in LCPUFAs (e.g. 20:3, 20:4 and 20:5) at the expense of shorter SFAs or MUFAs (e.g. 15:0, 16:0 and 16:1) on NGM plates (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by lipidomics data in Figure 4E.

claim: acs-13(et54) acts as a paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor because it promotes an increased abundance of PUFA-containing membrane phospholipids.
source: We conclude that acs-13(et54) acts as a paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor because it promotes an increased abundance of PUFA-containing membrane phospholipids, which is a mechanism by which to restore membrane fluidity in the paqr-2 mutant (Ruiz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on lipidomics data and prior knowledge.

claim: ACSL1 is at least 20-fold more highly expressed than ACSL5 and ACSL6 in HEK293 cells.
source: Based on qPCR, ACSL1 is at least 20-fold more highly expressed than ACSL5 and ACSL6 in HEK293 cells, and all three genes can be successfully knocked down using siRNA (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by qPCR data in Figure 5A-B.

claim: ACSL1, ACSL5 and ACSL6 can be successfully knocked down using siRNA in HEK293 cells.
source: Based on qPCR, ACSL1 is at least 20-fold more highly expressed than ACSL5 and ACSL6 in HEK293 cells, and all three genes can be successfully knocked down using siRNA (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by qPCR data in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Under basal conditions, silencing of ACSL1, −5 or −6 has no effect on membrane fluidity in HEK293 cells.
source: Under basal conditions, silencing of ACSL1, −5 or −6 has no effect on membrane fluidity (Figure 5C–D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by FRAP data in Figure 5C-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Silencing ACSL1 prevents membrane rigidification in HEK293 cells challenged with 400 μM palmitate.
source: However, silencing ACSL1 prevents membrane rigidification in HEK293 cells challenged with 400 μM palmitate (Figure 5E–F)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by FRAP data in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Silencing ACSL5 or ACSL6 had no effect on preventing membrane rigidification by palmitate in HEK293 cells.
source: silencing ACSL5 or ACSL6 had no such effect (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by FRAP data in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HEK293 cells challenged with palmitate have improved fluidity across the entire cell when ACSL1 is knocked down, as measured by the Laurdan dye method.
source: Using the Laurdan dye method, which reports on water penetration into the membrane that usually correlates with membrane packing and fluidity (Owen et al., 2012; Ruiz et al., 2019), confirms the FRAP results: HEK293 cells challenged with palmitate have improved fluidity across the entire cell (hence also in organellar membranes) when ACSL1 is knocked down (Figure 5G–I)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Laurdan dye data in Figure 5G-I.

claim: There was no difference in membrane fluidity measured by Laurdan dye in basal media where membrane homeostasis is not challenged.
source: there was no difference in basal media where membrane homeostasis is not challenged (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Laurdan dye data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Silencing ACSL1 abrogates the increased palmitate sensitivity of AdipoR2 siRNA-treated HEK293 cells.
source: Here, we found that silencing ACSL1 abrogates the increased palmitate sensitivity of AdipoR2 siRNA-treated HEK293 cells. Specifically, 200 μM palmitate causes membrane rigidification in HEK293 cells where AdipoR2 is silenced but not when both AdipoR2 and ACSL1 are simultaneously silenced (Figure 5J–L).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by FRAP data in Figure 5J-L.

claim: ACSL1 knockdown acts as a suppressor of AdipoR2 knockdown in HEK293 cells.
source: In other words, ACSL1 knockdown acts as a suppressor of AdipoR2 knockdown, just as the acs-13(et54) loss-of-function allele acts as a paqr-2(tm3410) suppressor in C. elegans.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the FRAP data.

claim: Silencing ACSL1 in HEK293 cells lowers their UPR activation when challenged with 400 μM palmitate.
source: Using qPCR to monitor the expression of UPR response genes, we found that silencing ACSL1 in HEK293 cells lowers their UPR activation when challenged with 400 μM palmitate, though there was no difference in cell viability (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by qPCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: There was no difference in cell viability when ACSL1 is silenced in HEK293 cells challenged with palmitate.
source: Using qPCR to monitor the expression of UPR response genes, we found that silencing ACSL1 in HEK293 cells lowers their UPR activation when challenged with 400 μM palmitate, though there was no difference in cell viability (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Trypan blue staining data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: No obvious changes in expression of other ACSLs were observed when ACSL1 is silenced in HEK293 cells challenged with palmitate.
source: However, no obvious changes in expression of other ACSLs were observed when ACSL1 is silenced in HEK293 cells challenged with palmitate, though their relative abundance vis-à-vis ACSL1 have strongly increased (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by qPCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: ACSL1 expression itself was not changed when silencing AdipoR2 or TLCD1/TLCD2.
source: Additionally, it is interesting to note that ACSL1 expression itself was not changed when silencing AdipoR2 or TLCD1/TLCD2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by qPCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Silencing of ACSL1 leads to a dramatic increase in PUFA-containing membrane phospholipids, with strong increases in the abundance of 20:4, 22:5 and 22:6 in both PCs and PEs of HEK293 cells challenged with palmitate.
source: Lipidomics analysis shows that, as in C. elegans, silencing of ACSL1 leads to a dramatic increase in PUFA-containing membrane phospholipids, with strong increases in the abundance of 20:4, 22:5 and 22:6 in both PCs and PEs of HEK293 cells challenged with palmitate (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by lipidomics data in Figure 6A.

claim: ACSL1 siRNA slightly increased PUFA levels in lysophosphatidylcholines in HEK293 cells challenged with palmitate.
source: and also slightly increased PUFA levels in lysophosphatidylcholines (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by lipidomics data in Figure 6B.

claim: The relative abundance of several types of sphingolipid classes, namely ceramides, dihydroceramides and glucosylceramide, were decreased by ACSL1 siRNA in HEK293 cells challenged with palmitate.
source: The relative abundance of several types of sphingolipid classes, namely ceramides, dihydroceramides and glucosylceramide, were also decreased by ACSL1 siRNA; levels of sphingomyelins and lactosylceramides were unaffected (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by lipidomics data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: Levels of sphingomyelins and lactosylceramides were unaffected by ACSL1 siRNA in HEK293 cells challenged with palmitate.
source: The relative abundance of several types of sphingolipid classes, namely ceramides, dihydroceramides and glucosylceramide, were also decreased by ACSL1 siRNA; levels of sphingomyelins and lactosylceramides were unaffected (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by lipidomics data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: No changes in the PUFA levels within TAGs were observed in ACSL1 knockdown HEK293 cells challenged with palmitate.
source: No changes in the PUFA levels within TAGs, in PC/PE and cholesterol/PC ratios or in the actual abundance of several phospholipid classes (PCs, diacyl PEs, alkenyl PEs, phosphatidylinositols and phosphatidylserines) were observed in ACSL1 knockdown cells (Figure 6C–E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by lipidomics data in Figure 6C-E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: No changes in PC/PE and cholesterol/PC ratios were observed in ACSL1 knockdown HEK293 cells challenged with palmitate.

evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by lipidomics data in Figure 6C-E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Silencing ACSL1 in palmitate-challenged cells leads to a specific increase in the levels of PUFAs in several membrane phospholipid classes (PCs and PEs) while leading to a depletion of some sphingolipid classes and no changes in non-membrane lipids (e.g. TAGs).

claim: ACSL1 is strongly enriched in the mitochondria of HEK293 cells (about 20x enrichment compared to whole lysate).
source: Using subcellular fractionation and Western blotting, we found that ACSL1 is strongly enriched in the mitochondria of HEK293 cells (about 20x enrichment compared to whole lysate; Figure 7A–B)

claim: Some ACSL1 is associated with the ER in HEK293 cells though this appears to be a small minority of the protein (only 3x enrichment in the microsomal fraction).
source: Some ACSL1 is associated with the ER in HEK293 cells though this appears to be a small minority of the protein (only 3x enrichment in the microsomal fraction; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).

claim: There is a pronounced excess of palmitoylcarnitine in the mitochondria of ACSL1 siRNA-treated HEK293 cells challenged with palmitate.

evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by lipidomics data.

claim: There is a dramatic reduction in the HPLC peak containing cardiolipins in ACSL1 siRNA-treated HEK293 cells challenged with palmitate.

evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by HPLC and mass spectrometry data in Figure 7C-F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cardiolipins in ACSL1 siRNA-treated HEK293 cells challenged with palmitate contained slightly but significantly more 16:0 and 18:2 FA chains and significantly less 18:1 FA chains.

claim: Expression of several genes implicated in CL synthesis (CRLS1) and remodelling (Tafazzin and LCLATA1), was reduced in HEK293 cells treated with ACSL1 siRNA.

evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by qPCR data in Figure 7G.

claim: The downregulation of Tafazzin in ACSL1 knockdown cells is in agreement with a previously published study of a mouse ACSL1 knockout model.
source: the downregulation of Tafazzin is in agreement with a previously published study of a mouse ACSL1 knockout model (Grevengoed et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Mitochondrial respiration was not detectably different in HEK293 cells challenged with palmitate and treated with either control or ACSL1 siRNA.

evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Seahorse analysis data in Figure 7H-I and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-H.

claim: ACSL1 can be effectively silenced using siRNA in human umbilical cord vein endothelial cells (HUVEC).
source: We found that ACSL1 can be effectively silenced using siRNA in human umbilical cord vein endothelial cells (HUVEC) (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by qPCR data in Figure 8A.

claim: Silencing of ACSL1 did not affect membrane fluidity in HUVEC cells in basal conditions.
source: Using the previously described Laurdan dye method to monitor membrane fluidity (Owen et al., 2012; Ruiz et al., 2019), we found that silencing of ACSL1 did not affect membrane fluidity in basal conditions (i.e. in the absence of any challenge to membrane homeostasis) but did prevent membrane rigidification in HUVEC cells challenged with 400 μM palmitate (Figure 8B–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Laurdan dye data in Figure 8B-G.

claim: Silencing of ACSL1 prevented membrane rigidification in HUVEC cells challenged with 400 μM palmitate.
source: Using the previously described Laurdan dye method to monitor membrane fluidity (Owen et al., 2012; Ruiz et al., 2019), we found that silencing of ACSL1 did not affect membrane fluidity in basal conditions (i.e. in the absence of any challenge to membrane homeostasis) but did prevent membrane rigidification in HUVEC cells challenged with 400 μM palmitate (Figure 8B–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Laurdan dye data in Figure 8B-G.

claim: ACSL1 knockdown by itself does not overwhelm membrane homeostasis under basal conditions but does protect against the membrane rigidifying effects of palmitate both in HEK293 cells and in human primary endothelial cells.
source: ACSL1 knockdown by itself does not overwhelm membrane homeostasis under basal conditions but does protect against the membrane rigidifying effects of palmitate both in HEK293 cells and in human primary endothelial cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the results section based on the FRAP and Laurdan dye data.

claim: A CRISPR/Cas9 genome-wide screen identified ACSL3 as the top hit for decreasing palmitate toxicity in human cells, which acts by activating SFAs such as exogenously provided palmitate.
source: Our findings reinforce those of Zhu et al. who performed a CRISPR/Cas9 genome-wide screen to identify modifiers of palmitate toxicity in human cells (Zhu et al., 2019). Their top hit for decreasing palmitate toxicity was ACSL3, which acts by activating SFAs such as exogenously provided palmitate; mutating ACSL3 therefore decreases the incorporation rate of SFAs into phospholipids, hence helping to maintain membrane fluidity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: ACSL4 was the top hit for increasing palmitate toxicity in a CRISPR/Cas9 genome-wide screen, which acts by activating UFAs such that they can be incorporated into phospholipids.
source: Conversely, their top hit for increasing palmitate toxicity was ACSL4, which acts by activating UFAs such that they can be incorporated into phospholipids; mutating ACSL4 therefore decreases the incorporation rate of UFAs into phospholipids, and thus exacerbates the membrane-rigidifying effects of palmitate.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with reference to the Zhu et al. study.

claim: ACS-13 (in C. elegans) or ACSL1 (in human) act by activating LCFAs on mitochondrial membranes and promote their import into that organelle where they are utilized for mitochondrial membrane homeostasis or degraded.
source: Our work suggests a third mechanism by which ACSLs influence palmitate toxicity: ACS-13 (in C. elegans) or ACSL1 (in human) act by activating LCFAs on mitochondrial membranes and promote their import into that organelle where they are utilized for mitochondrial membrane homeostasis or degraded.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Mutating or inhibiting ACS-13 or ACSL1 results in more PUFAs available for incorporation into phospholipids, which improves membrane fluidity.
source: Mutating or inhibiting ACS-13 or ACSL1 results in more PUFAs available for incorporation into phospholipids, which improves membrane fluidity (see model in Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: Adipocyte-specific ACSL1 knockout mice exhibit a severe defect in mitochondria-based long-chain FA degradation.
source: Adipocyte-specific ACSL1 knockout mice exhibit a severe defect in mitochondria-based long-chain FA degradation, indicating that channeling LCFAs for degradation in mitochondria is an important function of ACSL1 in these cells (Ellis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Mouse cardiac myocytes lacking ACSL1 have decreased PUFA levels among mitochondrial phospholipids, including cardiolipins, accompanied by excess PUFAs in PCs and PEs.
source: Grevengoed and co-workers previously drew similar conclusions from a separate study: they found that mouse cardiac myocytes lacking ACSL1 have decreased PUFA levels among mitochondrial phospholipids, including cardiolipins, accompanied by excess PUFAs in PCs and PEs (Grevengoed et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Barth syndrome patients have severe cardiolipin deficiencies but are viable with cells capable of efficient respiration in spite of their abnormal mitochondria morphology.
source: Similarly, Barth syndrome patients have severe cardiolipin deficiencies but are viable with cells capable of efficient respiration in spite of their abnormal mitochondria morphology (Gonzalvez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Exploiting the differences among the ACSLs may allow the targeting of specific acyl-CoA synthetases, such as ACSL1, with small-molecule inhibitors and thus open new therapeutic avenues against lipotoxicity in clinical contexts such as dyslipidemia or liver steatosis.
